style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 6 gathers four warnings into one fatherly charge. First, get free from a rash pledge that has bound you to another man's debt -- chase your release like prey fleeing the hunter (vv. 1-5). Second, learn from the ant, who needs no overseer to provide against the cold, lest poverty raid you like an armed man (vv. 6-11). Third, beware the worthless troublemaker whose whole body signals deceit and whose ruin will come without remedy (vv. 12-15), capped by the LORD's list of seven things He hates (vv. 16-19). Finally the chapter returns to its great theme, the warning against the adulteress: keep your parents' teaching as a lamp, for the man who plays with this fire will not escape unburned, and a jealous husband's vengeance accepts no ransom (vv. 20-35).

1.text: My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, if you have shaken hands in pledge for a stranger,
1.amp: My son, if you have become surety [arab -- pledged yourself, stood as the guarantee for another's debt] for your friend [rea -- neighbor, companion], if you have struck [taqa -- driven in, clapped your hand to seal a bond] your hand [kaph -- palm] for a stranger [zur -- one outside, a foreigner to your trust],
1.notes: arab (H6148) is to give oneself as collateral for another man's obligation; taqa (H8628), normally to drive a tent-peg or blow a horn, here pictures the firm hand-clap that sealed a pledge (cf. 11:15; 17:18; 22:26-27). The danger is binding your own future to a debt you do not control.

2.text: you are snared by the words of your own mouth, taken captive by the words of your mouth.
2.amp: you are snared [yaqosh -- caught as in a fowler's trap] by the words [emer -- the very speech] of your mouth [peh], you are taken [lakad -- seized, captured] by the words of your mouth.
2.notes: yaqosh (H3369) and lakad (H3920) are hunting and warfare verbs -- the same mouth that gave the rash word becomes the trap and the captor. The doubled line drives home that the bondage is self-made, sprung by one's own promise.

3.text: Then do this, my son, and free yourself, since you have fallen into your neighbor's hand: go, humble yourself, and press your plea hard with your neighbor.
3.amp: Then do [asah] this, my son, and deliver [natsal -- snatch yourself free, rescue] yourself, since you have come [bo] into the hand [kaph] of your friend [rea]: go [yalak], humble [raphas -- stamp yourself down, make yourself low] yourself, and press boldly [rahab -- storm at him, importune urgently] upon your neighbor.
3.notes: natsal (H5337), the rescue-verb, opens a chain that runs through the passage (cf. v.5). raphas (H7511) is to tread oneself down -- a deliberate self-lowering -- while rahab (H7292) is to storm or act with force; together they urge the son to swallow his pride yet plead without let-up until the bond is loosed.

4.text: Let your eyes find no sleep, and let no drowsiness settle on your eyelids;
4.amp: Give [natan] no sleep [shenah] to your eyes [ayin], nor slumber [tenumah -- drowsiness, the first nodding-off] to your eyelids [aphaph];
4.notes: the urgency is total: shenah (H8142) is sleep, tenumah (H8572) the lighter doze. Do not even let your eyelids droop until the matter is settled -- the same restless diligence the sluggard of vv.9-10 so fatally lacks.

5.text: Free yourself like a gazelle from the hunter's hand, like a bird from the hand of the fowler.
5.amp: Deliver [natsal -- snatch yourself away, the verb of v.3] yourself like a roe [tsebi -- a gazelle, swift and wary] from the hand [yad] of the hunter, and like a bird [tsippor] from the hand of the fowler [yaqush -- the bird-trapper].
5.notes: natsal (H5337) returns to seal the appeal: escape as an animal bolts from the snare. The gazelle and the trapped bird picture a man who treats his entanglement not as a small embarrassment but as a hunter's net closing -- to be fled with everything in him.

6.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard; study her ways and grow wise.
6.amp: Go [yalak] to the ant [nemalah], you sluggard [atsel -- the slack, lazy man]; consider [raah -- look hard at, observe and learn] her ways [derek -- her habits, her manner of life] and be wise [chakam -- act with skill].
6.notes: the atsel (H6102), the sluggard, is sent to school under the smallest of creatures. raah (H7200) is more than a glance -- it is to look until one perceives; the tiny ant teaches the great lesson of self-governed diligence (cf. 30:25).

7.text: She has no commander, no officer, no ruler,
7.amp: She has no chief [qatsin -- captain, the one who decides], no overseer [shoter -- foreman, the one who drives the work], or ruler [mashal -- the one who holds dominion],
7.notes: qatsin (H7101), shoter (H7860), and mashal (H4910) name three ranks of authority the ant does without. The marvel is self-direction: she needs no one standing over her to make her provide -- the very oversight the lazy man assumes he requires before he will move.

8.text: yet she lays up her food in the summer and gathers her supply at harvest.
8.amp: yet she provides [kun -- prepares, makes firm and ready] her bread [lechem -- food, sustenance] in the summer [qayits], and gathers [agaph -- shuts up, stores against need] her food in the harvest [qatsir].
8.notes: kun (H3559) is to establish or make ready; agaph (H103, in the sense 'shut up/gather/store') is to lay up against a coming need. The ant reads the seasons -- working in the warmth so she will not starve in the cold -- a parable of foresight the sluggard refuses to learn.

9.text: How long will you lie there, sluggard? When will you rise up from your sleep?
9.amp: How long will you lie down [shakab -- stretch out, stay reclined] there, O sluggard [atsel]? When will you arise [qum -- get up, rouse and stand] out of your sleep [shenah]?
9.notes: shakab (H7901) is to lie prone; qum (H6965) is to rise and stand. The father's two questions corner the sluggard: not whether he will get up, but when -- the delay itself is the sin (cf. 26:14, the door turning on its hinges).

10.text: "Just a bit more sleep, a short doze yet, the hands crossed for a brief lying-down" --
10.amp: "A little [meat -- just a small amount] sleep [shenah], a little slumber [tenumah], a little folding [chibbuq -- a clasping] of the hands [yad] to lie down [shakab]" --
10.notes: the threefold meat (H4592), 'a little,' mimics the sluggard's own soothing self-talk -- each delay framed as harmless and brief. The folded hands are the very opposite of the working ant's; idleness dressed up as a small, reasonable rest.

11.text: and your poverty will come stalking in like a robber, and your need like an armed man.
11.amp: so your poverty [reysh -- want, destitution] will come [bo] like one who travels [halak -- a prowler on the road, a marauder], and your scarcity [machsor -- lack, the empty cupboard] like an armed man [ish magen -- a man behind a shield, a raider you cannot fight off].
11.notes: reysh (H7389) and machsor (H4270) are poverty and lack; magen (H4043) is a shield, so the want comes armed and unstoppable. The 'little' rests of v.10 add up to ruin that arrives suddenly and overpowering -- the harvest of the folded hands.

12.text: A worthless person, a man of wickedness, goes about with a crooked mouth;
12.amp: A worthless [beliyaal -- good-for-nothing, ruinous; the word later read as a name for the evil one] person [adam], a man [ish] of wickedness [aven -- iniquity, trouble], walks [halak] with a perverse [iqqesh -- twisted, bent out of true] mouth [peh];
12.notes: beliyaal (H1100) means utter worthlessness, a man who is himself a wreck and a wrecker. iqqesh (H6143) describes speech bent off the straight line of truth -- the catalog that follows shows wickedness written across the whole body, beginning at the mouth.

13.text: he winks with his eyes, signals with his feet, points with his fingers;
13.amp: he winks [qarats -- pinches the eye shut, gives the sly signal] with his eyes [ayin], he speaks [malal -- here, makes signs] with his feet [regel], he motions [yarah -- points, throws a sign] with his fingers [etsba];
13.notes: qarats (H7169) is the conspiratorial wink (cf. 10:10); the whole frame -- eyes, feet, fingers -- conspires in a coded language of deceit. The body that should serve truth becomes one continuous signal of hidden malice.

14.text: in his heart he plots evil, scheming mischief without end; he keeps sowing strife.
14.amp: perverseness [tahpukah -- twisted, upside-down dealing] is in his heart [leb], he devises [charash -- plows and forges in secret] evil [ra] continually [eth -- at every season]; he scatters [shalach -- casts out, flings] discord [madon -- contention, quarrels].
14.notes: charash (H2790) can mean to plow, to engrave, or to plot in silence -- the perverse man forges mischief quietly within (cf. 3:29). madon (H4066) is strife; he is a sower whose crop is conflict, flung out wherever he goes (the Hebrew literally 'casts forth' discord).

15.text: Therefore his ruin will come on him suddenly; in an instant he will be shattered, beyond all healing.
15.amp: Therefore his calamity [eyd -- disaster, the day of doom] will come [bo] suddenly [pitom -- in a flash, without warning]; in a moment [peta -- abruptly] he will be broken [shabar -- shattered, smashed to pieces] beyond remedy [marpe -- past all healing or cure].
15.notes: eyd (H343) is sudden calamity; the two words for suddenness (pitom H6597, peta H6621) hammer the unexpectedness. shabar (H7665), to shatter, with no marpe (H4832), no healing -- the schemer of v.14 meets a ruin as instant and irreparable as his plots were patient and hidden.

16.text: There are six things the LORD hates -- seven that are an abomination to His very soul:
16.amp: These six [shesh] things the LORD [YHWH] hates [sane -- holds in active hostility]; yes, seven [sheba] are an abomination [toebah -- a detestable thing] to His soul [nephesh]:
16.notes: the 'six... seven' is a numerical proverb (cf. 30:18,21) that means 'here is the full, climactic list.' sane (H8130) is no mild dislike but God's settled hatred; toebah (H8441) names what is loathsome to Him -- the sins are not merely forbidden but repugnant to His own nephesh (H5315), His very self.

17.text: eyes lifted up in pride, a tongue that deals in lies, and hands stained with the blood of the guiltless,
17.amp: haughty [rum -- lifted high, proud] eyes [ayin], a lying [sheqer -- false, deceitful] tongue [lashon], and hands [yad] that shed [shaphak -- pour out] innocent [naqi -- guiltless, blameless] blood [dam],
17.notes: the list runs head to foot, sin by sin: rum (H7311) eyes are pride lifted up (cf. v.13's signaling eyes); sheqer (H8267) is falsehood; the climax is yad that pour out naqi (H5355) blood -- murder of the guiltless, the gravest. Pride heads the list, for it is the root from which the rest grow.

18.text: a heart that forges wicked schemes, feet that run swiftly into evil,
18.amp: a heart [leb] that devises [charash -- forges, plots in secret] wicked [aven -- iniquitous] schemes [machashabah -- plans, calculated designs], feet [regel] swift [mahar -- in a hurry] to run [ruts -- race, sprint] to mischief [ra -- evil, harm],
18.notes: charash (H2790) echoes the schemer of v.14; machashabah (H4284) is the calculated plan. mahar (H4116) and ruts (H7323) picture not a man dragged into sin but one sprinting eagerly toward it (cf. 1:16; Isa 59:7) -- the heart designs and the feet race to carry it out.

19.text: a false witness who breathes out lies, and one who scatters strife among brothers.
19.amp: a false [sheqer] witness [ed] who breathes out [puach -- puffs forth, utters as easily as breathing] lies [kazab -- falsehoods], and one who scatters [shalach -- flings, casts out] discord [madon] among brothers [ach -- kinsmen].
19.notes: ed (H5707) is a courtroom witness; puach (H6315) means his lies come out as naturally as breath. The seventh and climactic abomination, set apart, is the strife-sower (madon, H4090, the same discord echoed from v.14) -- the man who breaks the bond among ach (H251), brothers, whom God means to dwell in unity (Ps 133).

20.text: My son, guard your father's commandment, and do not abandon your mother's teaching.
20.amp: My son, keep [natsar -- guard, watch over, protect] your father's [ab] commandment [mitsvah], and do not forsake [natash -- let drop, abandon] the law [torah -- instruction, teaching] of your mother [em];
20.notes: natsar (H5341) is the sentry's verb -- to mount guard over the parents' words as a treasure (cf. 2:8; 4:23). The mother's torah (H8451) is set in honored parallel with the father's mitsvah; the verse reopens the long warning against the adulteress by first arming the son with home instruction.

21.text: Bind them always upon your heart; tie them around your neck.
21.amp: Bind [qashar -- fasten, knot fast] them continually [tamid -- always, without a break] upon your heart [leb]; tie [anad -- wind, fasten about] them about your neck [garon -- throat, neck].
21.notes: qashar (H7194) and anad (H6029) recall the binding of God's words in Deut 6:8 -- not as outward charms but as truth fastened to the inner life (leb, H3820) and worn like an honored ornament. tamid (H8548), 'continually,' makes it a settled habit, not an occasional reach.

22.text: When you walk, it will lead you; when you lie down, it will watch over you; and when you wake, it will speak with you.
22.amp: When you walk [halak], it will lead [nachah -- guide, conduct as on a road] you; when you sleep [shakab], it will keep watch [shamar -- guard, preserve] over you; and when you awake [quts -- rouse, open the eyes], it will talk [siach -- muse and converse] with you.
22.notes: nachah (H5148) guides the traveler; shamar (H8104) guards the sleeper; siach (H7878) is meditative speech. The personified teaching becomes a living companion through the whole day -- a foretaste of the indwelling word that counsels the believer (cf. Ps 1:2; Col 3:16).

23.text: For the commandment is a lamp, the teaching is light, and the corrections of discipline are the way of life,
23.amp: For the commandment [mitsvah] is a lamp [ner -- a small light to walk by]; and the law [torah] is light [or -- daylight, illumination]; and the reproofs [tokachat -- searching corrections] of instruction [musar -- formative discipline] are the way [derek] of life [chay];
23.notes: ner (H5216) is the handheld lamp, or (H216) the broad light; together they pattern Ps 119:105. tokachat (H8433) and musar (H4148) name the bracing corrections that, far from killing joy, become the very derek (H1870) of life -- the road that leads to life, set against the adulteress's road to death (v.32; 7:27).

24.text: to keep you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress.
24.amp: to keep [shamar -- guard] you from the evil [ra] woman [ishshah], from the smoothness [chelqah -- the slippery flattery] of the tongue [lashon] of a foreign woman [nokriyyah -- a strange woman, off-limits];
24.notes: shamar (H8104) ties the home instruction back to its protective purpose. chelqah (H2513) is from a root for smooth/slippery -- her tongue is frictionless flattery; the nokriyyah (H5237) is 'strange' not by race but by being another man's or no man's, the recurring peril of chapters 2, 5, and 7.

25.text: Do not crave her beauty in your heart, and do not let her captivate you with her eyes.
25.amp: Do not desire [chamad -- covet, let appetite delight in] her beauty [yophi] in your heart [lebab]; neither let her take [laqach -- seize, carry off] you with her eyelids [aphaph -- the alluring glance, the painted lashes].
25.notes: chamad (H2530) is the covet-verb of the tenth commandment -- the sin is born in the heart before any act. laqach (H3947), to take/seize, makes her the predator and the man the captured; the warning strikes at the inward look, not merely the outward deed (cf. Matt 5:28).

26.text: For the price of a prostitute is a mere loaf of bread, but the wife of another man hunts the precious life itself.
26.amp: For by means of [baad -- on account of, through] a harlot [zanah -- the woman who plays the whore] a man is brought down to a piece [kikkar -- a round loaf] of bread [lechem]; and the adulteress [ishshah, the wife of a man] will hunt [tsud -- stalk as prey] for the precious [yaqar -- costly, irreplaceable] life [nephesh].
26.notes: zanah (H2181) is the verb 'to play the harlot.' The proverb sets two costs side by side: the prostitute leaves a man stripped to his last loaf, but the married woman's pursuit is deadlier -- she hunts (tsud, H6679) the yaqar (H3368) nephesh (H5315), the life itself, for adultery courts a husband's lethal vengeance (vv.34-35).

27.text: Can a man scoop fire into his lap and his clothes not be burned?
27.amp: Can a man [ish] take [chathah -- snatch up, especially live coals] fire [esh] into his bosom [cheq -- his lap, against his chest], and his clothes [beged] not be burned [saraph -- set ablaze, consumed]?
27.notes: chathah (H2846) is specifically to scoop burning coals. The rhetorical question makes adultery a physical impossibility to survive unscathed -- fire held to the body burns the body. saraph (H8313) is total consumption by flame; the image answers itself.

28.text: Or can a man walk on red-hot coals and his feet not be scorched?
28.amp: Or can a man [ish] walk [halak] upon hot coals [gachelet -- glowing embers], and his feet [regel] not be seared [kavah -- scorched, blistered]?
28.notes: gachelet (H1513) is live, glowing coals. The second image doubles the first (v.27): bosom and feet, holding and walking -- there is no way to handle this fire and come away unmarked. kavah (H3554) is to scorch; the burn is as certain as the contact.

29.text: So it is with the man who goes in to his neighbor's wife; no one who touches her will go unpunished.
29.amp: So is he who goes in [bo -- enters in to] to his neighbor's [rea] wife [ishshah]; whoever touches [naga -- so much as makes contact with] her will not be held innocent [naqah -- go unpunished, be acquitted].
29.notes: bo (H935), 'go in to,' is the standard idiom for sexual union. The fire-images collapse into the plain warning: naga (H5060), the lightest 'touch,' is enough, and naqah (H5352) -- to be cleared of guilt -- is exactly what the offender will never be. The burn of vv.27-28 is moral certainty, not mere risk.

30.text: People do not utterly despise a thief if he steals to fill his belly when he is starving,
30.amp: Men do not despise [buz -- hold in utter contempt] a thief [gannab], if he steals [ganab] to fill [male -- satisfy, make full] his soul [nephesh] when he is hungry [raeb -- famished];
30.notes: buz (H936) is scorn; the proverb concedes a measure of sympathy for theft driven by hunger -- the thief steals to feed a real need (male nephesh, to satisfy the appetite). This sets up the contrast of v.32: even the pardonable thief still pays, but the adulterer steals what no necessity required.

31.text: yet if he is caught, he must repay sevenfold; he must give up everything his house contains.
31.amp: But if he is found [matsa -- caught, discovered], he must restore [shalam -- repay in full, make complete] sevenfold [shibathayim]; he must give [natan] all the substance [hon -- wealth, goods] of his house [bayith].
31.notes: shalam (H7999), to make whole, is the restitution-verb; 'sevenfold' is the full, exhausting repayment that may cost the thief everything (hon, H1952) he owns. Even theft excused by hunger carries a ruinous bill -- the lesser sin still demands its price, so how much more the greater.

32.text: But the man who commits adultery with a woman is out of his mind; he who does it destroys his own soul.
32.amp: But whoever commits adultery [naaph -- breaks the marriage bond] with a woman [ishshah] lacks [chaser] understanding [leb -- heart, here the seat of sense]: he who does [asah] it destroys [shachath -- ruins, corrupts past repair] his own soul [nephesh].
32.notes: naaph (H5003) is the act of adultery itself; the man 'lacks leb' -- Hebrew locates good sense in the heart, so he is literally heartless, void of judgment. shachath (H7843) is to ruin or corrupt utterly: unlike the thief who loses goods (v.31), the adulterer destroys his own nephesh (H5315), his very life and self.

33.text: Wounds and disgrace are what he will find, and his shame will never be wiped away.
33.amp: A wound [nega -- a blow, an open hurt] and dishonor [qalon -- shame, public disgrace] he will get [matsa -- meet with, attain]; and his reproach [cherpah -- the lasting stain of scorn] shall not be wiped away [machah -- blotted out, erased].
33.notes: nega (H5061) is a stroke or plague; qalon (H7036) is humiliation. matsa (H4672), 'to find,' wryly echoes v.31 -- the thief is 'found' and pays, but the adulterer 'finds' only wounds and shame. The cherpah (H2781) cannot be machah (H4229) -- unlike a debt repaid, the disgrace leaves a permanent mark.

34.text: For jealousy enrages a husband, and he will show no mercy in the day of vengeance.
34.amp: For jealousy [qinah -- the burning zeal of a betrayed husband] is the rage [chemah -- hot fury, poison-heat] of a man [geber -- a strong man, a warrior]: therefore he will not spare [chamal -- show pity, hold back] in the day [yom] of vengeance [naqam].
34.notes: qinah (H7068) is the fierce protectiveness of wronged love (cf. Song 8:6); chemah (H2534) is wrath that burns like venom. The geber (H1397), the man in his strength, will not chamal (H2550) -- will grant no pity -- on the yom of naqam (H5359), the day he settles the account.

35.text: He will accept no compensation; he will refuse it, however large the bribe you offer.
35.amp: He will not regard [nasa panim -- lift up the face, show favor toward] any ransom [kopher -- a price paid to buy off vengeance]; nor will he be content [abah -- consent, be willing], though you multiply [rabah -- heap up, increase] the gift [shochad -- bribe].
35.notes: kopher (H3724) is the ransom-price that elsewhere may cover a wrong, but here no sum will buy the husband off -- he will not 'lift the face' (nasa, H5375; panim, H6440) of any offer. abah (H14) is to be willing; rabah (H7235) is to multiply -- even a mounting heap of shochad (H7810), bribes, leaves his fury unbought. The closing image seals the warning: this is a debt no money can settle.
